# Summary {#part-reasoning-summary .unnumbered}

Part IV treated reasoning as a problem of controlling computation: how much a model spends before its answer is fixed, and where it spends it. Several mechanisms provide that control. A prompt alone can sometimes elicit reasoning the model would not otherwise produce. A system can search over chains, trees, programs, solver calls, or proof scripts. A verifier can select among candidates, and training can make the model produce useful reasoning traces more consistently. A service can also spend extra computation at inference time on requests that appear hard.

Extra computation can improve coverage and selection. It can also hide failures, increase latency, and spend budget on tasks whose difficulty was never measured. The part therefore restated each reasoning claim as operational questions: where the extra work is paid for, who checks it, which trace is kept, and what rule stops the loop.

Across the part, a reasoning system is described by its budget, search space, verifiers, traces, and stopping rules. Routing remains the main unsolved problem: when test-time compute keeps helping, when it saturates, and how a production service should distribute a limited reasoning budget across real workloads. Part V turns the routing problem into concrete serving mechanisms, where latency, batching, cache residency, and price determine whether a product can offer the extra reasoning.
